paras: The Lowrysville lynching threat of 1903 was a reported move by a crowd at Lowrysville, Chester County, South Carolina, to lynch a Black man named Jim Montgomery, later called Jim Gilmore, in early May 1903. Governor Heyward sent the Lee Light Infantry from Chester by special train, and the sheriff took the prisoner to jail without resistance. Papers disagreed over how near a lynching had come, and the man drew renewed notice when he broke out of the Chester jail a month later.

According to the Chester Lantern, someone raised a window at the Lowrysville house of Mrs. Neely Smith, an aged widow, at about 1 a.m., presented a pistol and said he would shoot if an alarm was raised. Her granddaughter, Mamie Hardin, ran for the neighbors and the intruder fled. After daylight a track was followed to Will Simpson's place, where Montgomery was arrested because his shoes were believed to match it.

Montgomery was brought to Lowrysville, where, the Columbia State correspondent wrote, he was "locked up in a store and surrounded by armed men." By night it was thought there was danger of a lynching, and reports reached Chester, seven miles away, that a lynching was imminent. At the request of Solicitor Henry, Governor Heyward placed the Lee Light Infantry, 42 strong, under Sheriff Cornwell, and the company left on a special train.

The troops found no large crowd, and the sheriff met no resistance in claiming his prisoner, who was lodged in the Chester jail to await trial. The Lantern reported that he had confessed, but added that he admitted "at the point of a pistol" only that he was the right man and denied knowing anything about the deed.

Around the night of June 9-10 Gilmore and another prisoner, named as Bill Torbet, Will Talbert or William Tolbert, cut their way out of the Chester jail. A Lowrysville store and post office was broken into the next night, and a Lowrysville letter blamed the escapees, while Sheriff Cornwell offered $10 for each man. The Columbia Record put the state's cost of the militia service and special train at about $175.
In May 1904 Sheriff Logan and two civilians captured Gilmore at a saw mill near King's Mountain, and Sheriff Cornwell took him back to Chester. No report of a trial or sentence was found.

Only white papers covered the episode, nearly all of them in South Carolina, and no Black-press report was found. A Columbia wire printed in the Savannah Morning News under "LYNCHING THREATENED", and in the Atlanta Constitution and Keowee Courier under "Troops Are Guarding Negro", said the militia "probably prevented the lynching." The Columbia State's Chester correspondent instead headed his dispatch "Lynching did not occur" and presented the call-out as a step to preserve "Chester's reputation against all kinds of lawlessness."

After the jail break the tone hardened: a Lowrysville letter called him "the desperate negro" who had "barely escaped being lynched," and complained that he had been "too carelessly handled" in jail. That letter warned that such escapes "make men slow to commit such characters to the jail," while the Columbia Record headlined its item "Costly Jim Gilmore."

The two local Chester accounts played down the threat that the wire reported, the Lantern saying that "but few persons were violently disposed." The May reports name the man Jim Montgomery, while the June 1903 and 1904 items call him Jim Gilmore and tie him to the same militia call-out without explaining the change. The charge also grew vaguer in later retellings, from threatening a widow with a pistol to "attempting a dreadful crime" and breaking into a house of "unprotected ladies."

The 1904 Yorkville Enquirer placed the militia call after he was committed to the Chester jail, whereas the May 1903 reports have the troops going to Lowrysville to bring him to jail. The Chester dispatch dated May 2 places the excitement on the night of May 1, while the wire dated May 5 and the Lantern of the same day describe it as recent, so the exact date is uncertain.

reader.title: Lowrysville lynching threat of 1903
bases: A mob was reported gathering at Lowrysville to lynch an arrested Black man, and the governor sent a militia company to take him to jail; no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

No one was killed: the man was taken to the Chester jail by the sheriff and militia without resistance (A2, A3). The threat arose from an accusation of entering a widow's house with a pistol (A1, A3), but whether a mob actually formed is disputed (A2).

The arrest, the militia call-out and the removal to jail are reported independently by the Columbia State correspondent, the Chester Lantern and the wire (A1, A2, A3), but the State correspondent called the lynching report 'greatly exaggerated' and the Lantern found no large crowd (A2, A3), while the wire said the militia probably prevented a lynching (A1).

The Lowrysville letter called him 'the desperate negro', warned of a 'rude awakening' for the escapees, and complained he had been 'too carelessly handled' in jail.
The Columbia Record's 'Costly Jim Gilmore' stressed the $175 cost of protecting him.
